text: You are not smarter than Isaac Newton. So why did Newton lose a fortune on one stock?
vis: London street, crowd around a price board; Newton stares at it

text: He wasn't alone. America's most famous writer, its greatest economist, and two Nobel Prize winners all lost fortunes too. Four geniuses. The same four mistakes.
vis: Four portraits pop in one by one; four red crosses

text: And at the end, you'll meet a janitor who avoided all four, and died with eight million dollars.
vis: Janitor silhouette with a mop, $8,000,000 counter

text: Four true stories. Let's start with the smartest man of them all.
vis: Title: 4 geniuses who lost a fortune

title: 1|THE PHYSICIST|Isaac Newton · London, 1720
vis: Chapter card

text: London, seventeen twenty. Isaac Newton is seventy-seven years old. He has explained gravity, invented calculus, and for more than twenty years he has run the Royal Mint. He literally makes England's money.
vis: Newton walks through London; coins

text: That year, all of London is talking about one stock: the South Sea Company.
vis: Speech bubbles all saying SOUTH SEA

text: Its shares change hands in the coffee houses of a narrow street called Exchange Alley. From lords to servants, everybody wants in.
vis: Coffee house sign, crowd squeezing into an alley

text: The company has a monopoly on British trade with South America. The trade itself earns almost nothing. But the company has just made a deal to take over the national debt, and its share price is flying.
vis: Ship crossing to South America, empty chest; then price arrow up

text: In January, one share costs about a hundred and thirty pounds. By March, it's three hundred and thirty.
vis: Line chart Jan-Mar 1720

text: Newton owns shares. In April he sells them, for a profit of about twenty thousand pounds. A fortune. And a smart move.
vis: SELL marker on the chart; +£20,000

text: Except the price doesn't stop. By the end of May, it's five hundred and fifty. In early June, almost nine hundred.
vis: Chart keeps climbing past the SELL marker

text: And this is the part that hurts. Newton's friends are still in. Every week they get richer, and he just watches.
vis: Friends with growing piles of coins; Newton alone

text: So in June, the man who invented calculus does something very human. He buys back in. Near the top. With almost everything he owns.
vis: Newton pushes through the crowd and buys

text: In August, one share touches a thousand pounds. By the end of September, it's a hundred and fifty.
vis: Chart peaks at £1,000 and collapses

text: Thousands of investors are ruined. Parliament investigates, and sends the finance minister to the Tower of London. The same fortress where Newton's Mint makes its coins.
vis: Tower of London; minister behind bars; coin press

text: When it's over, his early profit is gone, and so is about a third of the fortune he started with. He later wrote that the South Sea had left his pockets empty.
vis: Wealth bars before/after; quote card

text: Notice what went wrong. It wasn't his math. Newton got out at the right time. What he couldn't stand was watching other people get rich without him.
vis: Newton portrait; chart with SELL (right) and BUY (wrong)

text: Mistake number one: following the crowd.
vis: Mistake card 1

title: 2|THE WRITER|Mark Twain · Hartford, 1880
vis: Chapter card

text: Hartford, Connecticut, eighteen eighty. Mark Twain is the most famous writer in America. Tom Sawyer is a hit. Huckleberry Finn is on the way. The money is pouring in.
vis: Twain in white suit on a New England street, books and coins

text: And Twain loves one thing almost as much as writing: new inventions.
vis: Twain with gears, light bulb, gadgets

text: By his own account, he was once offered stock in a strange new gadget, and said no. The gadget was the telephone.
vis: Mystery box, NO stamp, reveal: telephone

text: Then he meets an inventor named James Paige. Paige is building a machine that sets type for printing, automatically, faster than any human can.
vis: Paige with blueprint; machine of letters

text: Twain started out as a printer's apprentice, setting type by hand. He knows exactly how big this could be. Every newspaper on Earth would want one.
vis: Young Twain setting type; newspapers multiply

text: And he has money to spend. His own publishing company releases the memoirs of President Ulysses Grant, and they become a giant bestseller.
vis: Book stack growing, coins

text: So he invests. Then he invests again. And again. For fourteen years.
vis: Money bags fly into the machine; year counter 1880-1894

text: There's just one problem. The machine has around eighteen thousand parts, and it keeps breaking down. Paige keeps taking it apart to make it perfect. Every year, it's almost ready.
vis: 18,000 parts counter; machine smokes, parts fly

text: Meanwhile, a simpler machine called the Linotype is already at work in newspaper offices.
vis: Rival machine printing papers

text: By eighteen ninety-four, Twain has put in about three hundred thousand dollars, roughly ten million in today's money. The machine is a failure.
vis: $300,000 = about $10 million today; FAILED stamp

text: That same year his publishing company collapses, and Mark Twain files for bankruptcy.
vis: Twain alone in front of his house, BANKRUPT

text: He is almost sixty. So he sets off on a lecture tour around the entire world, to earn the money back. The law said he didn't have to repay his debts. He paid every dollar anyway.
vis: Globe with a route around the world; PAID IN FULL

text: Today, the only surviving machine sits in his old house in Hartford. As a museum piece.
vis: Machine on a pedestal behind a rope, MUSEUM label

text: Twain didn't follow a crowd. His mistake was different. He fell in love with one idea, and kept feeding it.
vis: Twain portrait; heart around the machine

text: Mistake number two: all your eggs in one basket.
vis: Mistake card 2

title: 3|THE ECONOMIST|Irving Fisher · New York, 1929
vis: Chapter card

text: Now, you could say Newton and Twain weren't money experts. This man was.
vis: Newton and Twain shrug; Fisher steps in

text: Irving Fisher is a professor at Yale, and the most famous economist in America. Other great economists would later call him the best the country ever produced.
vis: Fisher on the steps of the columned exchange, reporters around

text: He's also rich. He invented a filing system for index cards, sold it, and put the money into stocks.
vis: Index cards flip into cash, cash into share certificates

text: And in the nineteen twenties, stocks only seem to go up. Fisher's fortune reportedly reaches about ten million dollars.
vis: Dow chart 1921-1929 rising; $10,000,000 counter

text: But he isn't only investing his own money. He's also investing borrowed money. That's called leverage. In the nineteen twenties, you could buy stocks with as little as ten percent down.
vis: Small own pile + big borrowed pile; word LEVERAGE

text: Here's how it works. Put in ten dollars of your own, and borrow ninety. If the stock rises ten percent, you've doubled your money. If it falls ten percent, you've lost all of it.
vis: Leverage bars: $10 own + $90 borrowed; +10% and -10% cases

text: On October fifteenth, nineteen twenty-nine, Fisher announces that stock prices have reached, quote, what looks like a permanently high plateau.
vis: Newspaper quote card with date

text: Nine days later, the market crashes.
vis: Panic crowd in front of the exchange, board turns red

text: A few days after that, on two days in a row, the Dow loses nearly a quarter of its value.
vis: Two calendar pages Oct 28, Oct 29; -23%

text: For months, Fisher keeps telling investors that the recovery is just around the corner. He holds on.
vis: Fisher smiling while the line behind him falls

text: It isn't. By the summer of nineteen thirty-two, the Dow Jones has fallen eighty-nine percent from its peak.
Fisher's fortune is gone. He ends up deep in debt, borrowing from his sister-in-law. In the end, Yale has to buy his house and rent it back to him, so he has somewhere to live.
vis: $10M counter runs to zero and below; house with RENT sign

text: He spends the rest of his life working out why the Depression became so deep. His answer, a theory called debt deflation, is still used by economists today. He just had to live through it first.
vis: Fisher at a desk writing; DEBT DEFLATION book

text: The best economist in the country was wiped out. Not because he bought terrible companies. Because he bought them with borrowed money, and was sure he couldn't be wrong.
vis: Fisher portrait; borrowed pile crushes own pile

text: Mistake number three: leverage.
vis: Mistake card 3

title: 4|THE NOBEL WINNERS|Long-Term Capital · 1998
vis: Chapter card

text: Surely by the nineteen nineties, with computers and modern math, the geniuses had it figured out.
vis: Old computer, formulas floating

text: In nineteen ninety-four, a star Wall Street bond trader named John Meriwether starts a fund called Long-Term Capital Management.
vis: Glass office building, Meriwether and partners in suits

text: His team may be the smartest ever assembled in finance. It includes Myron Scholes and Robert Merton, who in nineteen ninety-seven share the Nobel Prize in economics.
vis: Team lineup; two get Nobel medals

text: Their strategy sounds boring. They find two almost identical bonds with slightly different prices, and bet that the gap will close. Each bet earns pennies.
vis: Two price lines converge; a penny drops

text: To turn pennies into fortunes, they borrow. A lot.
vis: Penny multiplied by a huge borrowed stack

text: And it works. The fund returns twenty-one percent in its first year. Then forty-three. Then forty-one.
vis: Bar chart 21%, 43%, 41%

text: By the start of nineteen ninety-eight, the fund has under five billion dollars of its own, and about a hundred and twenty-five billion borrowed. That's more than twenty-five dollars of debt for every dollar it owns.
vis: Tiny $4.7B block under a $125B tower; 25:1

text: Remember Fisher's math. At that level, a drop of just four percent in what the fund owns wipes it out.
vis: Tower shrinks 4%, own block disappears

text: Their models, built on years of market data, say a loss like that is almost impossible.
vis: Bell curve, tiny tail labelled almost impossible

text: Then, in August nineteen ninety-eight, Russia defaults on its debt. Investors everywhere panic. And the price gaps that were supposed to close get wider instead.
vis: Globe pin on Russia, DEFAULT; the two lines diverge

text: In less than four months, the fund loses four point six billion dollars.
vis: Counter: -$4,600,000,000; calendar pages

text: And because it owes so much, to so many banks, its collapse could take Wall Street down with it. So the Federal Reserve Bank of New York gathers the big banks in one room. Fourteen of them put in three point six billion dollars to take the fund over.
vis: Bankers in dark suits lined up in front of the columned building

text: The partners had about one point nine billion dollars of their own money in the fund. It's wiped out.
vis: $1.9B counter to zero

text: The fund is closed in early two thousand. Meriwether starts a second fund. It gets hit hard in the two thousand eight crisis, and closes too.
vis: CLOSED sign 2000; second sign 2009

text: The best-known book about them is called When Genius Failed. They trusted their models so much, they forgot a model can be wrong.
vis: Book cover (generic); cracked bell curve

text: Mistake number four: overconfidence.
vis: Mistake card 4

title: |THE PATTERN|What four geniuses have in common
vis: Chapter card

text: So. A physicist, a writer, an economist, and a room full of PhDs. Three centuries. Look at what they share.
vis: Timeline 1720, 1894, 1929, 1998 with portraits

text: None of them lost money because they were stupid. They lost it because they were smart. Smart enough to feel sure.
vis: Brain icon, word SURE

text: Newton followed the crowd. Twain bet everything on one idea. Fisher borrowed to buy more. And Long-Term Capital believed it couldn't be wrong.
vis: Four rows: portrait + mistake

text: The crowd. One basket. Leverage. Overconfidence. Almost every investing disaster in history is some mix of those four.
vis: Four mistake icons in a grid

text: And they still work today. The crowd is the stock everyone at work is talking about. One basket is all your savings in a single company, or a single coin. Leverage is trading on margin. And overconfidence is the thought: this time, I know.
vis: Four modern examples, one per mistake

text: So what does the opposite look like? Meet the least likely millionaire in America.
vis: Question mark turns into a mop

title: |THE JANITOR|Ronald Read · Brattleboro, Vermont
vis: Chapter card

text: Brattleboro, Vermont. Ronald Read pumps gas for twenty-five years. Then he works as a janitor in a department store for seventeen more.
vis: Read in the Vermont town

text: He drives a used car. He holds his coat together with a safety pin. Once, a stranger pays for his breakfast, thinking he can't afford it.
vis: Three small cards: car, safety pin, breakfast

text: When he dies in twenty fourteen, at ninety-two, his town finds out he was worth almost eight million dollars.
vis: Counter to $8,000,000

text: No formulas. No borrowed money. No hot tips. He bought shares in boring, solid companies. Soap. Medicine. Electricity. At least ninety-five of them.
vis: Crossed-out icons; grid of 95 small company tiles

text: He reinvested every dividend. And he held on. Some of his shares, for more than fifty years.
vis: Compounding curve over decades

text: He kept his stock certificates in a safe deposit box. When it was opened, the pile was five inches thick.
vis: Safe deposit box opens, tall pile of certificates, 5 in ruler

text: Check him against the list. The crowd? He ignored it. One basket? He had ninety-five. Leverage? None. Overconfidence? He never tried to outsmart anyone.
vis: Checklist: four mistakes, four green ticks

text: He left six million dollars to his town's hospital and library. The largest gifts either had ever received.
vis: Hospital $4.8M, library $1.2M

text: Newton could calculate the path of a comet. Ronald Read could wait. In the market, waiting won.
vis: Read on a bench at sunset, camera rises

text: You don't have to be a genius to build wealth. You have to be patient.
vis: Sunset over the town
